article_title: A Day in an All-Electric House.
brief_extract: Equally interesting was our visit to some toffee works, where we saw the toffee chopped into dainty squares, placed in a square of paper which moved along, neatly twisted one way, moved along again and finally shot out into a tin already half full. All this was done by electricity, and it was rendered doubly interesting by the fact that during the North-East Coast Exhibition, the stand belonging to the Co-operative Society was occupied in making toffee and was using an almost identical machine, so that every girl, for all had visited the Exhibition by school arrangement, had actually seen this toffee machine working. The bread-making industry shown by the film was very surprising.

location_standardised: Cheriton Fitzpaine, Devon, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Small village visited for its unique power station.
brief_extract: Our meetings during the past two months have been of a most interesting character. On May 1st, a party of sixteen members journeyed by motor-coach to Cheriton Fitzpaine, a village of 500 inhabitants about 20 miles out of Exeter. This small village, tucked away in the folds of the lovely Devon hills, possesses not only beauty and charm to greet the traveller, but also one of the smallest power stations in the country, supplying electricity for house and street lighting, thus dispelling one of the worst bugbears of country life—oil and candles.

location_standardised: Dartington Hall, Devon, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Estate visited for its village industry experiments.
brief_extract: Besides lighting the village, it also provides power to run the small butter factory and egg-testing station, where the produce of the many farms in the district is collected and made ready for market. On June 24th we were very happy in joining with the Torquay and Plymouth Branches in a visit to Dartington Hall. This is not an academy, an estate or an agricultural college, but an "experiment." The first aim of the owners is to endeavour to bring back to rural England the old-time village industries, and experiments are carried out in hand-weaving, woodwork and farming.

Soon after this, Miss Anne Helm gave a cookery demonstration to a large audience in the Lecture Theatre of the Technical Schools here. location_standardised: Torquay, Devon, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Location visited for a demonstration on electricity in health.
brief_extract: Partridge, on "Simple Household Repairs." Members showed great interest in this lecture, which made clear to them how much practical assistance they would obtain by being members of this Association. On May 5th, by kind permission, our members visited the Torquay Baths Saloon, where a demonstration was given on the restoration of health by the use of electricity. During the short existence of this Branch, we have been taught the practical uses of electricity by labour-saving in the home; money-saving, by learning to do our own simple household repairs; and the healing of the body.

Since the opening of the Branch, four lectures have been organised, dealing with such subjects as "What you should know about your Electrical Installation," simple explanations being given as to how various small repairs may be carried out, "Modern Architecture and Electric Lighting," "The Evolution of the Electric Cleaner," and "The Making of Artistic Lamp Shades." All these lectures have been very well attended, the average number at each one being between fifty and sixty.

location_standardised: Bradford, West Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom

brief_extract: Two electric cooking demonstrations have been arranged in conjunction with the Bradford Corporation Electricity Department, and we have had one outing to an All-Electric Farm; the forty members who attended found this to be most interesting and enjoyable. Arrangements are being made for a further visit to an Electric Poultry Farm, which will take place early in July. The Committee are endeavouring to compile a syllabus for the whole of the next Winter session, giving details of the lectures arranged, for distribution to the members.

brief_extract: The advantages and necessity of electrically-lighted house numbers are now being realised and there has recently been the suggestion that the greatest benefit would accrue to the householders if these house lights could be controlled simultaneously with the customary street lighting. In certain towns on the Continent lighted devices giving the house numbers are compulsory, and the idea of employing this method in England is an idea which will be welcomed on many building estates where the small house is predominant. Unlike many other nations, the community does not favour the large dwelling house, and our cities are rapidly spreading outward.

brief_extract: The age when we marvelled at the telephone is past. To-day it stands at our elbow, patient, sombre, and as unmoving as the faithful sentinel amid the ruins of Pompeii. location_standardised: Carluke, South Lanarkshire, Scotland, United Kingdom
brief_context: A thriving area served by the Clyde Valley Company.
brief_extract: One of the most important functions of the Clyde Valley Electric Power Company is the supply of electricity for lighting and heating purposes in outlying districts, and assisting in the industrial development of rural areas by making available an adequate source of electrical energy. The thriving areas around such centres as Carluke, Shotts, East Kilbride, Kirkintilloch, and Helensburgh, in some of which oil and tallow were the only means of illumination not so very long ago, indicate the transformation which the development of the company's schemes has meant to the scattered population in the entire valley of the Clyde. In addition to the facilities of electricity supply, however, it is a point of importance and interest that dwellers in rural areas are able to get the current at a rate which is comparable with that obtaining in the largest towns in the country.

article_title: Electric Clocks which Regulate and Wind Themselves.
brief_extract: It will be clear from what has been said that for the "Synclock" to keep exact time it is essential that the frequency should be precisely 50 cycles per second. Fortunately, with the advent of the "Grid," all modern electricity supply stations regulate their frequency so closely by reference to Greenwich Observatory that a "Synclock" connected to any wall socket can be relied upon to give true "Greenwich time" within a few seconds in the week. It thus becomes possible for everyone whose house is connected to an alternating current supply to instal these "Synclocks" in any room by merely plugging them into ordinary wall sockets.

It is interesting to speculate upon what the future may have in store for this old clock, built in the reign of William and Mary (only forty years, in fact, after the Fire of London) and electrified in the reign of King George V. brief_extract:
The Electrical Age 181
The New President, LADY MOIR, O.B.E.. Who presided at the Glasgow Conference and gave the following Address on "ELECTRICAL EDUCATION"
" We of the Electrical Association for Women should look upon it as a fortunate omen for future success that we were invited by our Glasgow and District Branch to hold our Conference in the first Civic and Empire Week of the City of Glasgow ; and also that this is the year the great discoveries of Michael Faraday are being celebrated. With such a happy combination we ought to try and make it an epoch year for our Association by some decided step forward.

location_standardised: Forth Bridge, Edinburgh, Scotland, United Kingdom
brief_context: Example of an engineering work lit by electric arc lamps.
article_title: The New President, LADY MOIR, O.B.E.
brief_extract: At that time the imagination of the country was occupied with the problem of locomotion—either by railways or canals. In my memory it was considered a novelty to see a great engineering work lighted by electricity—a notable example being the Forth Bridge, lit by electric arc lamps to make it possible to carry on the work of construction night and day ; and this was done summer and winter. Even then breakdowns were somewhat frequent, and I can recall Sir William Arrol when the arc lights failed admonishing his electric engineer and accusing him with kindly sarcasm of " looking for them with a candle." At that time no electric motor could be relied on for driving machinery with certainty.

location_standardised: Park Lane Hotel, Westminster, London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Site of the Electrical Association for Women's AGM.
article_title: The New President, LADY MOIR, O.B.E.
brief_extract: Electrical cranes were unheard of, and electrical pumps and machinery, so easily obtained to-day, were unprocurable. Lady Moir, O.B.E., was elected President of the Electrical Association for Women at the Annual General Meeting held at the Park Lane Hotel on April 17th. Lady Moir, who is a Past President of the Women's Engineering Society and a Founder Member of the Electrical Association for Women, has often described herself as an " Engineers by Marriage." As wife of one of the foremost Civil Engineers of the day, Sir Ernest Moir, Bart., she has travelled all over the world with her husband in his work in connection with the building of Bridges, Tunnels, Docks and Harbours.

The Glasgow Electricity Department has for many years pursued an energetic policy, and has been one of the outstanding Municipal undertakings in this country to consider the interests of the home-maker in regard to electricity. The Central Electricity Board commenced its operations of the "grid" in Glasgow, and this system, now rapidly being proceeded with, will do much to cheapen the cost of electricity in the home, owing to several important factors: It should greatly improve what is called the Load Factor, which means the amount of current continually being taken from any generating station, in comparison with its possible total output, and it will also standardise current supply, and by means of unification it will in the future make it possible for the housewife who may have to move her home from one part of the country to another to use the same appliances, and not be compelled, as is often the case to-day, to purchase new apparatus when moving to another district.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding concentration of industry and population.
brief_extract:
Now, the point which I wish to make is that,
while the Grid may not in the early stages make
any spectacular reduction in the price of electricity
to certain of the larger electricity supply under-
takings, although it will undoubtedly do so to
many of the smaller ones, it will provide a neces-
sary initial impetus which will result in the pro-
gressive lowering of the cost through increased
use in the manner which I have endeavoured to
explain to you. A fact which we all deplore, but which we have
been unable to prevent, is the increasing concen-
tration of industry and population in a number of
restricted areas in Great Britain. While this
original concentration possibly grew out of certain
natural advantages of the sites for various indus-
trial processes, the tendency in later times was for
the concentration to augment itself through the
advantages attaching to the cheaper communal
services in the form of electricity, gas, water, etc.,
which it was able to give.

always be able to purchase their electricity at the
most favourable rates, the operations of the Grid
will make electricity available at many parts of
the country at rates very little in excess of those
prevailing in the larger industrial centres.

location_standardised: Great Britain, United Kingdom
brief_context: Undertakings engaged in making frequency changes.
brief_extract:
Now, the point which I wish to make is that,
while the Grid may not in the early stages make
any spectacular reduction in the price of electricity
to certain of the larger electricity supply under-
takings, although it will undoubtedly do so to
many of the smaller ones, it will provide a neces-
sary initial impetus which will result in the pro-
gressive lowering of the cost through increased
use in the manner which I have endeavoured to
explain to you. A fact which we all deplore, but which we have
been unable to prevent, is the increasing concen-
tration of industry and population in a number of
restricted areas in Great Britain. While this
original concentration possibly grew out of certain
natural advantages of the sites for various indus-
trial processes, the tendency in later times was for
the concentration to augment itself through the
advantages attaching to the cheaper communal
services in the form of electricity, gas, water, etc.,
which it was able to give.

The Electrical Age 203

" A HAMELIKE TOUCH."

These Overhead Transmission Lines which are now known as the "Grid" do not disfigure the beauty of the countryside in the way their detractors would like one to believe. The views of unbiased observers like Sir Reginald Blomfield, the famous architect and artist, who has examined these transmission lines in many parts of the Continent, are that they give a touch of real interest to certain areas. Others again have likened them to a string of pearls round the neck of the countryside.

location_standardised: Perthshire, Scotland, United Kingdom

brief_extract: That, however, is an imaginative touch which I cannot just follow. One Perthshire farmer recently expressed the view that they "ga'ed a mair hamelike touch to the countryside." I do not know that he perhaps quite correctly expressed himself. What he probably wished to convey was that they were the medium which linked his remote countryside with more intensive civilisation.

brief_extract:
The important bodies connected with the
industry with the status of whom many
readers of this article may be acquainted,
for these include The Institution of Elec-
trical Engineers, The Association of Con-
sulting Engineers. The Incorporated Muni-
cipal Electrical Association, The British
Electrical and Allied Manufacturers' Asso-
ciation, The Electrical Contractors' Associa-
tion of England and Scotland, some years
ago appreciated the weakness of the public
in this respect, and the position in which
they oft-times found themselves by en-
trusting wiring work in their innocence to
persons who had no technical knowledge
of the art, or qualifications for carrying it
out, and whose only attraction was the
unblushing offer to undertake work at
prices which could not as a fact (though
the customer did not know it) cover prime
cost of a decent job, and which resulted in
their being obliged to take out the shoddy
work executed by the specious and incom-
petent, and replacing it with an installa-
tion by a competent contractor who knew
his job and its requirements. The poor
customer thus suffered not only inconveni-
ence, but the loss of his money, for he
found he was only throwing away good
money after bad if he attempted to recover
from the originator of his trouble, this
type of man seldom being worth powder
and shot.

brief_extract:
The Countrywoman

While a good deal has been done in the towns recently to improve the standard of lighting in the home, in country towns and villages where electricity does exist the standard is lamentably low. Realisation by women of the value of good lighting, and proof that they feel the lighting of roads outside the towns requires improvement, is indicated by the following Resolution which was recently passed by the Somerset Federation of Women's Institutes :

" That as the darkness in many of our villages is a danger, this meeting requests the National Federation of Women's Institutes' Executive Committee to urge on the Government the importance of electric light at a reasonable cost at the earliest possible moment."

Modern Decoration

Modern architecture and decoration encourage original ideas in illumination ; modern art, probably more than anything else stimulates the use and appreciation of good lighting. Rooms which are architecturally and decoratively pleasing are enhanced by harmonious lighting effects, while they would be entirely spoiled by incorrect lighting.

brief_extract: Cordially do I echo Miss Sharp's peroration "Save your money and reach the height of bliss. Have an all electric home." It occurred to me that a useful supplement to her article might be a description of my experience in converting an old-fashioned and inconvenient London house, by means of complete electrification, into an easily-managed and inexpensively-run home that requires practically no more labour than a modern flat. Mine is a very old house (I think about 150 to 160 years old) and when we took it over it was typical of the smaller London house in its old-fashioned and cumbersome general arrangement and in the expense of running it efficiently.

location_standardised: Basra, Basra Governorate, Iraq
brief_context: The final destination reached before the return flight.
brief_extract: In Baghdad, that city of the Arabian Nights, only the main street is paved and the others are mud, and many are so narrow that two horsemen could not pass ; but every corner is full of interest and the people in the streets, most interesting of all ; Bedouin in their desert robes, Jews, Turks with their amber beads, veiled women, babies with henna dyed hair and enamelled nails, beggars, camels, white donkeys, cafés where the Arabs sit cross-legged on couches by the roadside, and in the midst of it all the very efficient Traqui policeman at each crossroad, standing under their umbrellas and keeping order ! Leaving Baghdad at 5 a.m., we had a glorious flight to Basra, and flying low over the ruins of Ur of the Chaldees, we got a splendid idea of what the ancient city must have been. We saw all there was to be seen in Basra, including Sinbad's Tower, on the edge of the old sea bed.

Emerging from the Underground station at Earl's Court the view which greets the jaded traveller is not exactly one to arouse enthusiasm or aesthetic pleasure. brief_extract: We town dwellers had difficulty in accepting this and the fact that all the people in these hamlets had until recently used oil as their illuminant in houses, farms and churches. Yarm, with its market cross built in 1710, old Queen Anne houses and now with two saw mills run electrically; Hutton Rudby, with no water or sewage system until after electric supply was connected; Potto, a tiny hamlet of 163 persons; Swainby, a beautiful village with Potto Beck running through the village; Broughton, with the remains of a Roman settlement surrounded by hills with jet quarries—all these villages connected up electrically. The road into Helmsley took us right over the Cleveland Hills; the country was wild and beautiful.

location_standardised: Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Mentioned in context of old houses and the E.A.W. organization.
article_title: Outline of an address given at the first Conference of the Yorkshire County Organisation of the E.A.W. at Leeds
brief_extract: For general illumination I have planned in one room deep cream walls quite plain, with floodlights concealed in a cornice painted nigger-brown; above the cornice there is a multi-coloured frieze and a cream ceiling; the whole effect due to the soft shadows of the frieze is restful while excellent as a means of lighting. There is yet much to be done in finding the most attractive means of illuminating our houses; for example: a dark oak-panelled room with a low ceiling such as we find in our old Yorkshire houses presents difficulties. The copies of medieval sconces and lamp brackets which have been so generally used in such places can, I think, be bettered, and those of you who have a taste for design might well consider how you would deal with such a room.

article_title: Outline of an address given at the first Conference of the Yorkshire County Organisation of the E.A.W. at Leeds
brief_extract: Many of our members should find congenial occupation in such matters as these either as a regular occupation or as a hobby; there is a great field for skilled electrical decorators. In Leeds, I am glad to say, the School of Art has already co-operated with me in the covering and painting of some special silk lamp shades in a way which encourages me to think that great progress can be made with the aid of our educational organizations. I have limited my remarks to the decorative effect of electric light, but the principles I have ventured to set before you apply with equal force to other electrical apparatus, and the design and arrangement of these so as to obtain utility and beauty in the home should be of equal interest to all women.

location_standardised: Saighton, Cheshire, England, United Kingdom

article_title: A SUCCESS IN RURAL ELECTRIFICATION: Impressions of a Visit to the Chester Rural Electrification Scheme
brief_extract: Although it was only possible in a short time to visit a few of the 300 farms connected up to the electricity supply, a very good idea was obtained of the work which is being carried out under this scheme. In a Saighton farm a large Ferranti tank supplies hot water for the household, and every kind of farm operation, including the scalding of pigs; the reliable hot water supply enables this operation to be carried out most effectively and the very high reputation of the pork from this farm is attributed to the electric water heating. The Electrical Age 403

Rowntree's "poverty line," would require 41/3 a week, and anything less quite definitely means inadequate or sub-standard provision for basic human needs. This estimate includes an allowance of 9/- a week only for rent and nothing at all for such items as smoking, papers, stamps, or even train fares, and in London and other large cities the rent allowance would be found inadequate. location_standardised: England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Where the Hungarian courier worked before the war.
brief_extract: We entered Budapest at midnight and my first impression was of a city of a thousand stars with Venus shining over all, thus fulfilling the promise of the Spirit of Romance which Budapest always holds in fiction. The Hotel had sent an English-speaking Hungarian courier to meet us and he became our general factotum; he had been a jockey in England before the war and was delighted to practice his English. He took me sightseeing when no other companion was available and his enthusiasm for his country made him a very agreeable guide.

location_standardised: Széchenyi Thermal Bath, Budapest, Hungary
brief_context: A prominent thermal bath mentioned for its splendor.
brief_extract:
With tea one is given the choice of lemon, milk or rum, and in one Hungarian household no tea was served, only wine. The swimming baths, of which there are several in Budapest, are the most wonderful in the world - there are hot sulphur baths, salt springs, magnesia and lithium springs; the Municipal Széchenyi Bath is like a royal palace. The beautiful Danube, so seldom blue, with its mountain landscape and noble palaces, the mingling of the East with the West in its buildings and monuments, the stately Parliament House, the four beautiful bridges, all these give Budapest the well-earned title of the "Queen of the Danube."
Space will not permit me to dwell on their world-renowned cafes and gypsy bands, which play sad and gay airs alternately.

brief_extract: Her public work is very well known in the Liverpool district; she was one of the first members of the Liverpool South African War Relief Committee, and during the Great War she became Chairman of the 8th Irish Battalion King's Liverpool Regiment Comforts Fund, whose successful " After Care " work still continues. Her work for ex-Servicemen, both English and French, and their families and her help in the adoption of the devastated war area, Givenchy la Bassee, has resulted in her election to life-membership of the British Legion, of " La Fédération Nationale Française des Veuves et des Orphelins de la Guerre," and of " L'Union Nationale Française des Anciens Combattants." Mrs. Wilson is the only British woman to have received such distinctions.

A Recent Visit to Japan
by the DOWAGER LADY SWAYTHLING

IN A FASCINATING TALK TO WOMEN DEMONSTRATORS, THE DOWAGER LADY SWAYTHLING SPOKE OF THE INTERESTING MODERN DEVELOPMENTS IN JAPAN, MENTIONING PARTICULARLY THEIR ADOPTION OF ELECTRICITY, AND ITS IMPORTANCE IN THE NATIONAL LIFE. It was less than fifty years ago when the electric supply business in Japan began in the City of Tōkiō with the formation of the Tōkiō Electric Light Company Ltd., 1887. Development, however, was strikingly rapid and the way for the utilisation of electricity swiftly increased in all sections of the community for domestic use, shops, factories and farms, serving for lighting, heating and power, so that it has become a close and indispensible element in social life.

It is wonderful sometimes what can be done with electricity and careful planning, especially in the country districts. brief_extract:
The fact that the total
output of the National Mark egg pack-
ing stations in 1932 exceeded 384 million
eggs will give some idea of the need for
efficient equipment. The improvements in
the technique of egg testing, grading and
packing in this country have been so great
in the past few years that England and
Wales to-day stands in the forefront of the
world as regards the efficiency of the equip-
ment of its egg packing stations, and our
methods have been adopted in other
countries, especially in Germany where the
latest grading machine will deal with 10,000
eggs per hour. The old water mill is one of the familiar
sights of the English countryside.

brief_extract:
DIPLOMA IN ELECTRICAL HOUSECRAFT FOR TEACHERS
The Electrical Association for Women, as a result of many requests, has decided to award a Diploma in Electrical Housecraft to Teachers who have done pioneer work in teaching this subject in schools and colleges. The popular Summer Schools for Teachers, inaugurated by the Board of Education, together with the evidence of enthusiasm and the desire to learn the methods of electrical housecraft evinced by such courses as those arranged by Battersea and Chelsea Polytechnics and other Institutes and Colleges, have given initiative to this move. Until the end of the current year the Diploma for Teachers will be issued without examination, on the satisfactory completion of the special application form.

location_standardised: Birmingham, West Midlands, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Refers to the volume of water pumped through condensers there.
brief_extract: The steam condenses and is pumped out of the condenser as distilled water, and put back into the boilers, thus avoiding waste. The amount of cooling water passing through the tubes of the condenser has to be very large, because the exhaust steam even at pressures lower than atmospheric pressure still retains its latent heat, and as a matter of fact, the quantity of water pumped through the condensers in Birmingham amounts to about 650 tons of water per ton of coal burnt, and as we are consuming about 11,000 tons of coal per week the magnitude of the water supply can be easily realised. It will therefore be seen how very important this question of water is, and how absurd it is to suggest putting large generating stations at the pit mouth, where there is generally no water at all, in order to save a trifle on the transport of coal.

THE POSSIBILITY OF A NEW ERA! It is of tremendous import that the national Grid which has been constructed by the Central Electricity Board is now completed and that within a reasonable time electricity will be available in almost every part of Great Britain. Mr.

brief_context: Context for an anecdote about candles and electric light.
brief_extract: Beard, M.Sc., M.I.E.E. When staying at a remote country inn candles were provided to light us to bed. location_standardised: Scandinavia, Europe
brief_context: Region where the World Power Conference met in July.
brief_extract:
World Power

At a time when politicians, economists and statesmen are discussing the problems of World Trade and Industrial Depression, it is good to know that the technologist is also realising his responsibilities in connection with these problems. The World Power Conference, which has for its object "To consider how the sources of Heat and Power may be adjusted nationally and internationally," met in Scandinavia in July, when representatives from most of the countries of the world were present. In Denmark, Sweden and Norway the conditions of power resources were studied and discussed and a week-end visit to Finland revealed marvellous possibilities in this wonderful country with its enormous water power resources.

M. HUTCHINSON SENDS US THE REPLY OF
The enterprise of the Kingston-upon-Hull Authority has shown that Working Class Houses at a rateable value of not more than £15 may be supplied with electricity at an economic tariff. This question has for some time past been a very absorbing one for the house- holder and also for the Electricity Supply Authorities, but very considerable and satisfactory progress has been made during the last few years, and we are now in a position to answer it definitely ; the principal object of these comments is to give the result of practical experience of a fairly large scale trial, which provides a con- clusive argument in favour.
